welcome.title: Welcome to ProdTunnel
welcome.body: A quick pass over what everything does. Two minutes, and you can skip or replay it any time from the ? button.

add.title: Add a tunnel
add.body: A tunnel is one SSH connection. This button opens the form — let's look at what's in it.

add-auth.title: How you authenticate
add-auth.body: Password, a private key file, or an SSH agent like Pageant. Passwords and key passphrases go into the Windows Credential Manager, never into the app's own database.

add-socks.title: What the tunnel exposes
add-socks.body: Turn on a local SOCKS5 proxy and point a browser or curl at that port. You can also add static port forwards later, from the tunnel's row in the list.

add-jump.title: Hopping through another tunnel
add-jump.body: "Connect via" makes this tunnel connect through another one's live session — the usual bastion setup. Connecting the inner tunnel dials the whole chain for you, outermost first.

list.title: The tunnel list
list.body: Toggle a tunnel with the switch. The dashed line animates while traffic can flow. Expand Forwards to add port forwards live — no reconnect needed. Tunnels that hop through another are indented under their parent.

bulk.title: Search and bulk actions
bulk.body: Ctrl+F drops in a search box to filter by name or host — Esc closes it. Connect or disconnect everything at once from here too.

router.title: The proxy router
router.body: Per-tunnel SOCKS ports make you pick a tunnel per application. The router flips that around: one local port, and rules choose a destination per connection.

router-enable.title: Turning the router on
router-enable.body: It binds one SOCKS5 port on 127.0.0.1 only. A rule pointing at a tunnel that isn't up will connect that tunnel on demand, so you can leave everything disconnected and let traffic dial what it needs.

router-rules.title: Rules decide where traffic goes
router-rules.body: Ordered top to bottom, first enabled match wins. Match on a host wildcard, a regex, or an IP range, then send it through a tunnel, straight out (direct), or block it. Anything unmatched takes the default action.

router-proxy.title: Catching every app
router-proxy.body: Tick this and Windows itself is pointed at the router, so every app follows your rules with no per-app setup. It's undone when the router stops — including after a crash.

router-log.title: Why did that go direct?
router-log.body: Every proxied connection is logged with the rule that decided it. This is the first place to look when a rule doesn't fire the way you expected.

capture.title: Capturing an app that has no proxy setting
capture.body: RDP clients, CLI tools, DB clients — most apps have nowhere to type a proxy address. Capture launches one with a small hook injected, so its traffic reaches the router anyway. Rules decide where it goes from there, same as anything else.

capture-launch.title: Launching a captured process
capture-launch.body: Point it at an .exe (Browse or paste a path), add arguments if it needs them. Recently launched targets show up as quick-relaunch buttons above the form.

capture-active.title: What's running
capture-active.body: Every captured process stays listed here with its PID, so you can stop one without hunting for it in Task Manager.

capture-log.title: Where its traffic actually went
capture-log.body: Each connection a captured process makes shows up here with the rule's decision — same idea as the router's own decision log, scoped to just this process.

settings-reconnect.title: Staying connected
settings-reconnect.body: Keepalives are how a dead connection gets noticed at all; retries back off so a flapping server isn't hammered. Local ports stay held during an outage so nothing else can take them.

settings-config.title: Moving to another machine
settings-config.body: Export writes your tunnels, router rules, and settings to one file. Secrets are only included if you set a passphrase — leave it blank and the file is safe to share.

tray.title: It lives in the tray
tray.body: Closing the window only hides it — tunnels keep running. Reopen from the tray icon, toggle tunnels from its menu, and use the tray's Exit item when you actually want to quit.
